\chapter{Where A Thing Is}
\label{ch:ml-place-words}
\hlchaptermodality{84}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is on, under, in front of or behind something else.}

From cold: all four place-words, the owner-ending the noun in front of them must carry, and the in-ending visible inside three of the four.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mukaḷil]{\ml{മുകളിൽ} (mukaḷil) — on top of}

\label{lesson:ML-C84-mukalil}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for a chair. Then put the owner-ending on it — the one \textbf{\ml{അമ്മ}} took.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the owner-ending comes first}]
\textbf{\ml{മുകളിൽ}} — \emph{mukaḷil} — on top of, above.

The track has given you a chair, a book and several other things in a room, and \textbf{no way to say where any of them is.} This is the first of four words that fix that, and the rule they all share is worth more than any one of them.

\textbf{The thing you are measuring from goes into the owner-form, and the place-word follows it.}

\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{മുകളിൽ}} — \emph{kasērayuṭe mukaḷil} — on top of the chair.

Read it literally and the logic is plain: \textbf{the chair's top-part}. Malayalam is not saying \emph{on} the chair; it is naming a part that belongs to the chair and putting you there. That is why the owner-ending is needed — without it the two words are not connected at all.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ}} & the chair's \\
\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{മുകളിൽ}} & on top of the chair \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So this costs you no new grammar either. \textbf{The owner-ending is the one from the genitive chapter, unchanged}: \textbf{\ml{കസേര}} takes \textbf{-\ml{യുടെ}}, just as \textbf{\ml{അമ്മ}} did there.

Put a thing in front and you have a sentence's worth:

\textbf{\ml{പുസ്തകം} \ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{മുകളിൽ}} — the book is on top of the chair.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mukaḷil}
  \item \emph{kasērayuṭe mukaḷil}
  \item what the chair had to take before the place-word could follow
  \item \emph{pustakaṁ kasērayuṭe mukaḷil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{mukaḷil} mean? (\textbf{On top of}.) What must the noun before it carry? (\textbf{The owner-ending}.) And what is \emph{kasērayuṭe mukaḷil} literally? (\textbf{The chair's top-part}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tāḻe]{\ml{താഴെ} (tāḻe) — below}

\label{lesson:ML-C84-thaazhe}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{on top of the chair}, and say what the chair had to take first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{താഴെ}}
\textbf{\ml{താഴെ}} — \emph{tāḻe} — below, under, down.

It is the opposite of the word before it, and \textbf{it takes exactly the same shape around it}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{മുകളിൽ}} & on top of the chair \\
\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{താഴെ}} & under the chair \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The owner-ending does not change and the order does not change. \textbf{Only the place-word swaps}, which is the whole point of learning the pattern before the words: each new one after this costs a word and nothing else.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tāḻe}
  \item \emph{kasērayuṭe tāḻe}
  \item \emph{kasērayuṭe mukaḷil}, then \emph{kasērayuṭe tāḻe}
  \item what changed between those two, and what did not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{tāḻe} mean? (\textbf{Below, under}.) Does the noun in front of it behave any differently? (\textbf{No — the same owner-ending}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[munnil pinnil]{\ml{മുന്നിൽ} \ml{പിന്നിൽ} (munnil, pinnil) — in front of, behind}

\label{lesson:ML-C84-munnil-pinnil}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{on top of} and \emph{below}. You have the up-and-down pair; these two are the other axis.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മുന്നിൽ}, \ml{പിന്നിൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{മുന്നിൽ}} — \emph{munnil} — in front of.

\textbf{\ml{പിന്നിൽ}} — \emph{pinnil} — behind.

Both go where the other two went, after a noun carrying the owner-ending, and the set is now closed:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{മുകളിൽ}} & on top of \\
\textbf{\ml{താഴെ}} & below \\
\textbf{\ml{മുന്നിൽ}} & in front of \\
\textbf{\ml{പിന്നിൽ}} & behind \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{മുന്നിൽ}} — in front of the chair. \textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{പിന്നിൽ}} — behind the chair.

The two new ones are a near-pair on the page as well as in meaning: \emph{munnil} and \emph{pinnil} differ in their \textbf{first} sound and agree in everything after it. Say them one after the other until the opening is what you hear, because that opening is the only thing carrying the difference.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{munnil}, then \emph{pinnil}
  \item which sound is the only difference between them
  \item \emph{kasērayuṭe munnil}
  \item \emph{kasērayuṭe pinnil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which one means \emph{in front of}? (\emph{\textbf{munnil}}.) Which means \emph{behind}? (\emph{\textbf{pinnil}}.) And how many place-words do you now own? (\textbf{Four}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[evide enna ōrmma]{(where a thing is) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R84-place-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all four place-words, up and down first, then front and back.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one shape, four fillers}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{മുകളിൽ}} & on top of the chair \\
\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{താഴെ}} & under the chair \\
\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{മുന്നിൽ}} & in front of the chair \\
\textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{പിന്നിൽ}} & behind the chair \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the first column downward. \textbf{Only the last word ever changes.} The noun takes the owner-ending and stays put, and each new place-word costs a word and nothing else — which is why the chapter spent its first lesson on the shape rather than on the vocabulary.

And the owner-ending is not new either. It is the one from the genitive chapter, picking its form by the last sound of the noun exactly as it did there, because \textbf{\ml{കസേരയുടെ} \ml{മുകളിൽ} is literally \emph{the chair's top-part}.} Malayalam does not say \emph{on} the chair — it names a part that belongs to the chair and puts you in it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Look at the ends of the four words themselves.

\textbf{\ml{മുകളിൽ}}, \textbf{\ml{മുന്നിൽ}} and \textbf{\ml{പിന്നിൽ}} all finish in \textbf{-\ml{ിൽ}} — the in-ending you have had since the first verbs. These are not really postpositions at all in origin: they are \textbf{part-words already sitting in the in-form}, which is why \emph{the chair's top-part} reads the way it does.

\textbf{\ml{താഴെ} does not.} It ends in \textbf{-\ml{െ}} and it means the same kind of thing.

So the pattern is real and \textbf{it covers three of the four}. That is worth stating plainly rather than tidying away: a pattern that explains most of a set is still useful, and the reader who notices the exception has read correctly rather than made a mistake. \textbf{Learn the shape from the three, and learn \ml{താഴെ} as it stands.}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all four place-words in a row
  \item \emph{kasērayuṭe mukaḷil}, then swap the last word three times
  \item \emph{pustakaṁ kasērayuṭe mukaḷil}
  \item which three of the four end in the in-ending, and which one does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the noun before a place-word carry? (\textbf{The owner-ending}.) Which of the four does not end in the in-ending? (\emph{\textbf{tāḻe}}.) And what changes when you swap one place-word for another? (\textbf{Nothing else}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
